items.prompt: What's the key test this unit uses to distinguish being tired from being burned out?
choices: How many hours of sleep someone got the previous night

Whether rest actually resolves it — ordinary tiredness recovers with genuine rest and the person's relationship to the work returns to normal; burnout's cynicism and reduced-efficacy components largely persist even after real, adequate rest
How long someone has been at their current job
Whether the person complains about being tired out loud
items.explanation: The distinguishing test isn't severity, it's whether rest resolves the state. Burnout specifically includes components (cynicism, reduced efficacy) that aren't about depleted energy, so rest alone — which directly addresses only exhaustion — doesn't fully resolve them.
items.reference:
Tired

Rest restores the prior relationship to work

Burned out

Cynicism & reduced efficacy persist after rest

Why: the test is resolution by rest, not severity.
items.learnMore:
Why severity is the wrong axis

It's tempting to treat burnout as just 'very tired.' The unit's model rejects that: tiredness and burnout differ in kind, not degree. A genuinely exhausting week that resolves after a weekend is ordinary tiredness, however intense it felt in the moment. Burnout is defined by two additional components — cynicism and reduced efficacy — that have nothing to do with energy levels, so no amount of rest touches them directly.

This is why 'take a vacation' is such an unreliable fix for burnout specifically: it treats the one component (exhaustion) that rest actually helps, while leaving the other two — the ones doing most of the damage to how someone experiences their work — untouched.

items.prompt: Someone takes a genuine week fully off, comes back feeling physically rested, but still finds themselves cynical about whether their work matters. What does this most likely indicate?
choices: The vacation was too short to count
They were probably just tired, not burned out
The exhaustion component resolved, but this is a sign that cynicism and/or reduced efficacy — components rest doesn't address — are also present
This is normal for everyone after any vacation and doesn't indicate anything
items.explanation: Physical rest resolving while cynicism persists is exactly the pattern that distinguishes burnout from ordinary tiredness — it shows the exhaustion component responded to rest while the other two components, which rest doesn't touch, remained.

items.prompt: Per L1/L2, does exhaustion alone (with no cynicism or reduced efficacy) constitute burnout in the fuller sense this unit describes?
choices: Yes — exhaustion alone is sufficient to define burnout

No — burnout specifically requires cynicism/depersonalization and reduced efficacy alongside exhaustion; exhaustion alone is a strong signal of ordinary overwork or poor sleep, not the fuller burnout pattern
No, because burnout doesn't include exhaustion as a component at all
Yes, but only if the exhaustion has lasted more than a year
items.explanation: The three-component model requires all three (or at least exhaustion plus one of the other two, per the loosely-converged research this unit summarizes) — exhaustion in isolation is exactly the kind of sign that's genuinely ambiguous between ordinary tiredness and something more serious, which is why the other two components matter for distinguishing them.
items.reference:
🔥 Exhaustion — overlaps with ordinary tiredness
😏 Cynicism — detachment from the work
📉 Reduced efficacy — effort genuinely stops working

Why: burnout needs the latter two, not just exhaustion.
items.learnMore:
Three components, not one number

Most burnout research converges on three components: exhaustion (energy depleted), cynicism/depersonalization (detachment and negative attitude toward the work), and reduced efficacy (a real, not just perceived, decline in the sense that effort accomplishes anything). Exhaustion is the only one of the three that overlaps with ordinary tiredness — which is exactly why it's the least useful component on its own for telling the two states apart.

Someone deep in a hard but healthy sprint can be genuinely exhausted without a trace of cynicism or reduced efficacy — that's overwork, not burnout. The other two components are what separate 'this is a hard week' from 'something is changing in how I relate to this work.'

items.prompt: A colleague says, 'I've been staying up way too late for a demanding launch, but I still love the work and feel like it's paying off.' Which components are present?
choices: All three: exhaustion, cynicism, and reduced efficacy
Exhaustion only — cynicism and reduced efficacy are explicitly absent from what they describe
Cynicism and reduced efficacy, but not exhaustion
None of the three components are present
items.explanation: They describe depleted energy (exhaustion) but explicitly deny detachment ('still love the work') and reduced efficacy ('feel like it's paying off'). Per the model, that's ordinary overwork, not burnout in the fuller sense — worth watching if it continues, but not yet the fuller pattern.

items.prompt: How does this unit connect to `sustainable-performance/myth-linear-output`'s idea that net output can decline as hours worked increase?
choices: It doesn't — the two units cover unrelated topics
Burnout is presented as a plausible mechanism behind that decline: exhaustion degrades focus, cynicism degrades the care put into work, and reduced efficacy removes the motivation to course-correct
Burnout is presented as the ONLY possible cause of declining output, with no other contributing factors
The connection is that burnout only happens to people who work fewer than 30 hours a week
items.explanation: L1/L2 tie the three burnout components to the negative-returns mechanism from the earlier unit — not as the sole explanation, but as a real, plausible contributor operating over a longer time horizon than a single overworked week.
items.reference:
🔥 Exhaustion → more errors
😏 Cynicism → less care catching them
📉 Reduced efficacy → less motivation to fix

Why: three compounding contributors to declining net output.
items.learnMore:
A longer-timescale mechanism

The negative-returns unit shows net output bending downward as hours worked keeps rising, driven by fatigue-induced errors compounding into rework. That's a within-week or within-sprint effect. Burnout is a plausible mechanism for the same shape playing out over months: exhaustion raises the moment-to-moment error rate, cynicism erodes the care that would normally catch those errors before they ship, and reduced efficacy removes the motivation to even try course-correcting once a problem becomes visible.

These three effects compound rather than simply add, which is part of why burnout's output cost can look disproportionate to the hours actually being worked by the time it's visible.

items.prompt: Per this unit, which burnout component most directly explains why someone stops trying to fix a problem even after they've noticed it?
choices: Exhaustion, because tired people physically cannot type
Reduced efficacy — a genuine sense that effort doesn't accomplish anything removes the motivation to course-correct even once an issue is visible
Cynicism, because cynical people are lazy by nature
None of the three components relate to motivation to fix problems
items.explanation: Reduced efficacy is specifically about the felt (and real) connection between effort and results. When that connection feels broken, noticing a problem doesn't reliably lead to acting on it, because the expected payoff of acting has itself eroded.

items.prompt: In the L1 scenario, why does thinking 'am I just being dramatic?' after a sarcastic comment make recognition harder, not easier?
choices: It doesn't — self-questioning always helps you catch problems earlier
Because that exact self-doubt is itself part of the cynicism pattern, so it tends to dismiss a real sign rather than genuinely evaluate it
Because sarcasm is never actually a real warning sign
Because asking any question at all delays recognition by definition
items.explanation: The self-doubt isn't neutral fact-checking — it's generated by the same cynical, detached mindset the sign is pointing at, so it's biased toward dismissal rather than genuine evaluation. That's the trap: the tool being used to check the sign is compromised by the thing it's checking.
items.reference:
1️⃣ Early cynicism appears
2️⃣ Cynicism ALSO questions itself: "am I dramatic?"
3️⃣ Dismissed as not real

Why: the trap uses the same compromised instinct to judge itself.
items.learnMore:
A self-referential trap

Most warning signs get evaluated by a part of you that isn't itself affected by the thing being evaluated. Burnout's cynicism component breaks that separation: the same detachment that produces the sign ('sure, this will fix everything') also colors the judgment about whether the sign is worth taking seriously ('am I just being dramatic'). It's not a coincidence that both come from the same place — that's precisely what makes this condition harder to self-diagnose than most.

The practical fix isn't to trust the self-doubt less in general — it's to check specific, named signs against a fixed list instead of relying on an in-the-moment judgment call, since that judgment call is exactly the part that's compromised.

items.prompt: What is this unit specifically scoped to teach?
choices: How to treat burnout once it's severe, including clinical intervention
How to redesign a team's workload and staffing to prevent burnout organizationally
How to recognize the specific, checkable pattern early, in yourself or someone you work with — the prerequisite step before any treatment or systemic fix
How to convince a manager that burnout doesn't really exist
items.explanation: The unit is explicit that treatment and systemic/organizational fixes are real and often the actual root cause, but out of scope here — this unit is about the specific skill of recognizing the pattern early, since that recognition is the necessary first step before any fix can be applied.
items.reference:
✅ In scope: recognizing the pattern early
❌ Out of scope: treatment, systemic/organizational fixes

Why: recognition is the prerequisite step, not the whole solution.
items.learnMore:
Why recognition is a separate skill

It's tempting to treat 'recognize burnout' and 'fix burnout' as the same problem, but they require different things. Recognition is a checklist-and-self-honesty skill anyone can build regardless of their position. Fixing the underlying cause — whether that's personal (boundaries, rest, seeking a different role) or organizational (staffing, workload, deadlines) — often requires authority, resources, or negotiation the recognizer alone may not have.

Separating the two matters practically: someone who's built the recognition skill but has no power to change their workload isn't failing at this unit's goal — they've done the necessary first step. What happens next is a genuinely separate problem, often not solvable by the same person alone.

items.prompt: Per this unit, what's the difference between saying 'I feel burned out' and saying 'I'm exhausted and increasingly cynical, and that specific combination is what burnout looks like'?
choices: There's no meaningful difference — both convey the same information

The second is specific and named, which is harder to dismiss (by others, or by yourself) than a vague feeling — the practical skill this unit builds is replacing vague feelings with specific, checkable signs
The first is always more accurate because it's simpler
The second is worse because it uses jargon
items.explanation: A vague statement invites an equally vague, dismissive response ('everyone's tired'). Naming the specific components present makes the claim concrete and harder to wave off — that precision is exactly the practical skill this unit is building.
items.reference:
❌ Vague: "I feel burned out" → easy to dismiss
✅ Specific: "exhausted AND increasingly cynical" → harder to dismiss

Why: specific, named signs beat a general feeling.
items.learnMore:
Precision as a practical tool

'I'm burned out' is a conclusion, and conclusions are easy to argue with ('no you're not, everyone's tired right now'). 'I'm noticing exhaustion and cynicism together, and that specific combination is the pattern this describes' is evidence plus a named framework — much harder to wave off with a generic response, because it invites engagement with the specific claim rather than the vague label.

This precision matters both for self-recognition (checking a specific list beats trusting a mood) and for communicating it to someone else who might be able to help address the cause.

items.explanation: Waiting for undeniable severity means the pattern has had more time to progress and compound (as the self-referential trap allows it to). Concrete, named signs make earlier recognition possible, before the cost of the delay accumulates further.

items.prompt: Per L2's diagram comparing 'tired' and 'burned out,' what happens on the burnout branch after rest?
choices: Full recovery, identical to the tired branch
Energy partially recovers, but cynicism and reduced efficacy remain largely unchanged
Nothing changes at all, including energy levels
The person becomes more exhausted than before the rest
items.explanation: The diagram shows the two branches diverging specifically at the outcome of rest: the tired branch fully recovers, while the burnout branch only partially recovers (the exhaustion part), with cynicism and reduced efficacy staying largely unchanged.
items.reference:
😴 Tired --rest--> fully recovered
🔥 Burned out --rest--> energy partial, cynicism/efficacy unchanged

Why: the two branches diverge at what rest actually fixes.
items.learnMore:
Reading the divergence

L2's flowchart deliberately shows two branches starting from a similar-looking state ('depleted, needs a break') and diverging based on what happens after rest is applied. This is the practical, checkable version of the abstract 'is it tired or burned out' question: don't ask it in the abstract, apply genuine rest and observe which branch the outcome matches.

The catch, covered later in the unit, is that this test takes time to run — days or a week of real rest — so it's a confirming test after the fact, not a fast diagnostic in the moment. The component checklist is the faster, in-the-moment alternative.

Because rest is always fully effective for any kind of fatigue
Because L2 doesn't actually make this distinction anywhere
items.explanation: Intensity ('how tired, 1-10') is the same axis for both ordinary tiredness and burnout — both can feel severe. The test that actually separates them is behavioral: does a real break restore the person's prior relationship to the work, or not.

items.prompt: Per L2's table, what does 'needing more effort than before for routine tasks' represent, on its own?
choices: Definitive proof of full burnout by itself
The early sign of the exhaustion component specifically — genuinely ambiguous on its own between ordinary overwork and the start of the fuller burnout pattern
The late-stage sign of the cynicism component
Something unrelated to any of the three components
items.explanation: L2's table lists this as exhaustion's early sign. Since exhaustion alone doesn't distinguish burnout from ordinary overwork, this specific sign is genuinely ambiguous by itself — it's the combination with cynicism and/or reduced efficacy that makes the fuller pattern clear.
items.reference:
ComponentEarly sign
ExhaustionMore effort for routine tasks
CynicismOccasional sarcastic detachment
EfficacyVague sense effort hasn't amounted to much

Why: each row alone is ambiguous; the combination is the signal.
items.learnMore:
Reading the early-sign column correctly

L2's table lists an early and late version of each component, but the columns aren't meant to be read as three independent checklists to tally separately. The point of the early-sign column is to be checked deliberately, before the late-sign column becomes undeniable — and the point of having three rows, not one, is that any single row's early sign is individually ambiguous.

'More effort for routine tasks' alone could be a rough sprint. 'More effort for routine tasks' plus 'occasional sarcastic detachment' together, both present at the same time, is a meaningfully stronger signal — that's the combination this unit keeps returning to.

A settled belief that the work will never matter regardless of outcomes
items.explanation: L2's table lists the late-stage cynicism sign as a consistent, default assumption of futility going into any effort — a step further than the early stage's occasional sarcastic comment.

items.learnMore:
Why the early column matters more

The late-sign column exists mostly as a warning of what the unaddressed early sign becomes, not as the primary thing to check for. By the time a component reaches its late-stage form (default futility, persistent depletion, a settled belief nothing matters), it's typically visible without any deliberate checking — which is exactly why this unit's practical skill is built around noticing the early column, deliberately, before it progresses that far.

Reading the table left-to-right (early → late) is meant to make the progression concrete: it isn't three unrelated states, it's the same component intensifying if the underlying driver isn't addressed.

L2 argues this makes burnout harder to self-diagnose than most other health-adjacent issues, because the mechanism doing the detecting is the same mechanism producing the thing to be detected. A broken bone doesn't make you skeptical about whether it's really broken. Cynicism does exactly that to itself — it colors both 'is this a real problem' judgments in general and the specific judgment about its own warning signs.

The practical consequence: don't trust an in-the-moment 'would I know if this were serious' feeling here. Check against the fixed, specific list instead, precisely because the feeling is the compromised part.

items.learnMore:
The four-month gap, mechanistically

Path A and Path B are constructed to hold every fact constant except recognition, isolating exactly one variable. Month 2's exhaustion, month 3's cynicism, month 4's flat sense of accomplishment — identical events on both timelines. What diverges is entirely internal: Path A rationalizes each one away individually ('just a demanding sprint,' 'normal venting,' 'I'll feel it after a real weekend'), which is the self-referential trap from L2 playing out three separate times. Path B checks each sign against the fixed list instead, notices the combination forming by month 3, and names it precisely enough that a manager conversation the same week leads to a real fix by month 4.

The four-month gap isn't a difference in how bad the underlying situation was — it's the compounding cost of delayed recognition, which is exactly what this unit is trying to make checkable rather than left to instinct.

items.prompt: Per L3's third failure mode, why didn't Path A's genuine, fully-disconnected week off resolve the underlying problem?
choices: Because the vacation wasn't long enough — a longer vacation would have fully resolved it

items.explanation: L3 explicitly frames this as a mismatch between the fix (rest, which addresses exhaustion) and the actual problem (all three components, driven by unsustainable load) — Path B's eventual recovery came from addressing the load directly, not from rest alone, which is exactly what Path A's experience already demonstrated wouldn't be sufficient.

❌ Cynicism, reduced efficacy → unaddressed by rest

items.learnMore:
Why 'take a vacation' is a mismatched default

Vacations are the most common, most socially acceptable response to visible strain — which is exactly why they're a trap when applied without checking which components are present. Path A's week off delivered exactly what rest can deliver: physical recovery of energy. It could not deliver what it was never going to touch: the cynicism and reduced-efficacy components, which are about the person's relationship to the work, not their energy level.

Path B's eventual fix — deprioritizing a feature, adding a second engineer to share on-call — worked because it addressed the actual driver (unsustainable load) rather than substituting a generically pleasant intervention (rest) for a specific one. The lesson generalizes beyond burnout: match the fix to the diagnosed cause, not to whichever fix is easiest to offer.

items.learnMore:
Calibrating confidence to evidence

This failure mode is about a specific kind of overreaction: treating the first noticed sign as if it already settles the question. Path B's month-2 handling is the model to copy — flag it, watch for the others, but don't declare burnout on exhaustion alone, since exhaustion alone is exactly the sign type most easily explained by ordinary causes (a hard sprint, bad sleep, a stressful week).

The opposite failure — waiting for all three components to be undeniable before taking any sign seriously — is just the self-referential trap in a different shape. The calibrated middle is: one sign, watch; two or more together, name it and act.

This is the same distinction the unit's scope statement makes in L1, showing up again as a failure mode in L3: recognition and response are two different steps, and this unit only teaches the first one.
